{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2025}}
'''Marshall P. Tulin''' (14 March 1926 – 31 August 2019) was an American engineer working in [[Fluid dynamics|hydrodynamics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mcdermottcrockett.com/tribute/details/144504/Marshall-Tulin/obituary.html|title=Obituary of Marshall Peter Tulin &#124; McDermott-Crockett & Associates Mortuary}}</ref> He was the Director of the Ocean Engineering Laboratory, [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], where he also held a University of California President Chair Professorship from 1982 to 1987.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sad News - Professor Emeritus Marshall Tulin |url=https://chancellor.ucsb.edu/memos/2019-09-26-sad-news-professor-emeritus-marshall-tulin |access-date=November 11, 2024 |publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara |date=September 26, 2019}}</ref> His pioneering work in the 1950s is credited with successful developments in the theory of [[supercavitation]] for naval engineering.

After graduating from [[MIT]] in 1946, he first worked on high-speed [[wind tunnel]] testing of the [[Bell X-1|X-1]] aircraft before moving to work for the Navy at the [[David Taylor Model Basin]]. He founded a consulting company, Hydronautics Inc, with [[Phillip Eisenberg]] in 1959.

He was elected to membership of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1979.<ref>{{cite news |title=Professor Marshall P. Tulin |url=https://www.nae.edu/28436/Professor-Marshall-P-Tulin |access-date=11 November 2024 |publisher=United States National Academy of Engineering}}</ref>

==Selected writing==

* Tulin, M. P. (1963). Supercavitating flows - small perturbation theory. Laurel, Md, Hydronautics Inc.
* Tulin, M. P., & Hsu, C. C. (1982). Theory of high speed displacement ships with transom sterns. Laurel, Md, Hydronautics Inc.
